I make a silly mistake in defining ramification index in my own repo :( :( :( (yes the definition in #mathlib4 > Improving the definition of ramification index? should be equivalent to the correct definition). Clearly that's because I didn't read Neukirch's Algebraic Number Theory book carefully.

Say L/K is an algebraic extension with K‾\overline{K}K the algebraic closure. Let v be an R\mathbb{R}R-valued absolute value on L and let w be any extension of it to K‾\overline{K}K (whose existence is still WIP, but stated in Neukirch's book). Then there are inertia subgroups IL⊆Gal(K‾/L)⊆Gal(K‾/K)I_L\subseteq\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{K}/L)\subseteq\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)IL​⊆Gal(K/L)⊆Gal(K/K) and IK⊆Gal(K‾/K)I_K\subseteq\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{K}/K)IK​⊆Gal(K/K) for w defined in the usual way (which also works for infinite places).

  • My definition of ramification index (https://github.com/acmepjz/lean-iwasawa/blob/master/Iwasawalib/NumberTheory/AbsoluteValue/RamificationIndex.lean) is the index of ILI_LIL​ inside IKI_KIK​ (which is well-defined in the sense that one may replace K‾\overline{K}K by any normal extension of K containing L, whose proof depends on some WIP sorry). Pro: this definition is also correct for infinite places.
    Unfortunately, this is (probably) not correct in the following cases:

    • if L/K is (purely) inseparable: in such case the index of ILI_LIL​ inside IKI_KIK​ is always 1 but v is ramified
    • if the residue field extension is not separable
    • if v is non-archimedean and not discrete (I don't know why it causes problems)

    Excluding the above cases, this definition should be the same as the definition below (as well as the current definition in mathlib or in the above link), for example if L/K is normal, then the index of ILI_LIL​ inside IKI_KIK​ should be equal to the size of I(L/K) which is the kernel of Gal(L/K) to the Galois group of residue field, and the whole thing should come from docs#Ideal.ramificationIdx_mul_inertiaDeg_of_isLocalRing.

  • The definition of ramification index in Neukirch's book is the index of v(K×)v(K^\times)v(K×) in v(L×)v(L^\times)v(L×). Pro: does not need to choose w. Pro: isUnramified_iSup can be proved easily, probably? Con: for infinite places, another definition is required. Con: I don't know what will happen if v is not discrete.

For now I need some suggestions for design decisions. For experiment, maybe I'll create a branch to nuke my incorrect definition and use the definition in Neukirch's book instead.

Maybe I should stick to my own definition, for the following reasons:

  • The definition of unramified extension using inertia subgroup is used in Iwasawa's paper On Γ-extensions of algebraic number fields, especially for infinite extensions.

  • This definition diverges from the valuation-theoretic definition in infinite case, but IMO the valuation-theoretic definitions goes weird in that case. For example, consider nontrivial finite extensions Q‾p/L/K/Qpunr\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/L/K/\mathbb{Q}_p^{\mathrm{unr}}Q​p​/L/K/Qpunr​ between the maximal unramified extension and the algebraic closure of Qp\mathbb{Q}_pQp​. The inertia subgroup definition tells us that such extension is (totally) ramified, which coincides with intuition (there are no nontrivial unramified extensions above maximal unramified extension).

    However, if consider K=Qp(μ∞,p1/n∣n≥1)K=\mathbb{Q}_p(\mu_\infty,p^{1/n}\mid n\geq 1)K=Qp​(μ∞​,p1/n∣n≥1) then the valuation-theoretic definition tells us that Q‾p/K\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/KQ​p​/K is unramified since v(Q‾p×)=v(K×)=Qv(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p^\times)=v(K^\times)=\mathbb{Q}v(Q​p×​)=v(K×)=Q. This seems unreasonable!

Is all of this a solution in search of a problem?

Are there people out there talking about ramification index in these contexts? Is your question "here are several proposals for ramification index, all of which give the right answer in all the cases that mathematicians care about (finite extensions L/K where K is finite over the field of fractions of a complete DVR with perfect residue field) and all of which give different junk answers away from this case, which one shall we use?"

Or is your question "I know that people are using the concept of ramification index (i.e. using a number to understand a subtle phenomenon) outside of these standard situations and we need to be careful to conform with what these people are doing?"

My recollection is that @Adam Topaz once said that ramification index should just be the index of the image of v inside the image of v', where v' on the top extends v on the bottom. Probably 0 is a good choice when the index is infinite. Do you have an explicit objection to this definition of the form "I have seen places in the literature where the concept of ramification index is actually being used and this definition gives the wrong answer"?

Or is your question "I know that people are using the concept of ramification index (i.e. using a number to understand a subtle phenomenon) outside of these standard situations and we need to be careful to conform with what these people are doing?"

I think this is closest to my question. My problem is to write a correct definition of unramified extension to be used in the formalization of Iwasawa's theorem on growth of class groups. It's natural to check Iwasawa's original paper and follow the definitions in it. Now there are something divergent from the standard definition in number theory book. I have no objection to the definition you proposed (which is the same as in number theory book). I just want to remind myself that it's subtle outside standard situations.

Note that the definition of unramified extension also affects downstream definitions, e.g. maximal (abelian) extension of a field unramified outside S. I'm worried on the cases that such field happens to be an infinite extension of Q.

For example, in Iwasawa theory, if K∞/KK_\infty/KK∞​/K is a Zp\mathbb{Z}_pZp​-extension, one often consider the maximal unramfied abelian extension (or maximal abelian extension unramified outside p) of K∞K_\inftyK∞​. IMO you must choose which definition you should use, since they divergences in this case, since there exists a valuation on K∞K_\inftyK∞​ above p which is non-discrete (since there exists a prime of K above p which has infinite ramification index in K∞K_\inftyK∞​, a standard result in Zp\mathbb{Z}_pZp​-extension).
What happens if you just use the definition in the other thread?
I guess is the issue that you want a definition that unifies the infinite places with the finite places?

Consider an extreme case: Q‾p/L/K/Qp\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/L/K/\mathbb{Q}_pQ​p​/L/K/Qp​ where KKK is such that v(K×)=Qv(K^\times)=\mathbb{Q}v(K×)=Q and OK/mK=F‾p\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{m}_K=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_pOK​/mK​=Fp​. Then v(K×)=v(L×)=Qv(K^\times)=v(L^\times)=\mathbb{Q}v(K×)=v(L×)=Q hence the valuation definition gives ramification index 1. The length definition in #mathlib4 > Improving the definition of ramification index? also gives ramification index 1, since one easily checks mKOL=mL\mathfrak{m}_K\mathcal{O}_L=\mathfrak{m}_LmK​OL​=mL​. But the inertia subgroup definition gives ramification index e=[IK:IL]=[L:K]e=[I_K:I_L]=[L:K]e=[IK​:IL​]=[L:K], since IKI_KIK​ is equal to Gal(Q‾p/K)\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p/K)Gal(Q​p​/K) because the residue field of K is already F‾p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_pFp​.

I know that the valuation definition coincides with the inertia subgroup definition for discrete valuation case. But I don't know if there are problems in non-discrete valuation case.

For K∞K_\inftyK∞​ in Iwasawa theory application, the v(K∞×)v(K_\infty^\times)v(K∞×​) is not discrete (while not being equal to whole Q\mathbb{Q}Q yet). Its residue field over a place above p is still finite, though. The above case that these two concepts differ occurred when the valuation group is the whole Q\mathbb{Q}Q and the residue field is F‾p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_pFp​. But I feel that it may also occurred for our K∞K_\inftyK∞​ (I can't think of a proof that they agree on such situation).

I see -- thanks a lot for explaining!

So you are saying "here is an example (which we might not care about) to show that two naive definitions of "unramified" might disagree in an exotic situation. Now let's consider Iwasawa theory, where we definitely want to consider unramified extensions of big fields like K∞K_\inftyK∞​. Are we sure that mathlib is returning e=1e=1e=1 iff an extension is unramified in the sense that Iwasawa means?" So in fact there is a mathematics question here.
